To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

human papillomaviral DNA integrates in the cellular genome in regions always associated with known oncogenes or tumor phenotypes, and that the integration sites of DNA viruses can be used for mapping the location of genes involved in tumor phenotypes.
the integration of human papilloma virus (HPV) DNA in the human genome is not a rare event, but occurs in a large number of cells in the normal epithelium.
the integration sites of human papilloma viruses in human cervical carcinomas are located in chromosomally defined regions always associated with known oncogenes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular biology of human papilloma viruses and their role in cervical cancer.
the study of the molecular basis of human papilloma virus‐associated oncogenesis.
the identification of genes in chromosomal regions associated with papillomavirus integration.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the integration sites of human papilloma virus DNA in cervical carcinoma can be used as a starting point for the isolation of oncogenes or tumor suppressor genes.

the integration of HPV DNA into the human genome is the first step in the development of cervical carcinoma and that integration of the viral genome into the cellular DNA is necessary but not sufficient for the development of cervical cancer.
human papillomaviral DNA integration in chromosomal DNA is a common event in the development of cervical carcinomas.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
human papillomaviral integration sites can be used to locate genes implicated in the tumorigenesis of human papilloma‐associated tumors.
the integration of papillomaviruss in the human genome can lead to the deregulation of cellular genes, which can be involved in the development of cervical cancer.

papillomaviridae are the only DNA viruses that can cause human cancer, that they are not transforming viruses, that they are dependent on cellular factors to cause cancer, and that they are not oncogenes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
human papillomoviruses, in addition to being a causative agent in cervical cancer, are a tool for identifying genes involved in oncogenesis.
the viral DNA is not the cause of cancer, but rather the integration of the viral DNA into the host cell genome is what triggers cancer.
integration sites can be used as a marker for chromosomal regions that contain genes involved in the tumor phenotype, a situation similar as for non‐transforming viruses.
